stories.title: Assam's flood toll nearly triples in a day to 31 dead, as the Brahmaputra breaches danger levels in 12 districts
stories.what_happened: The Assam State Disaster Management Authority said the flood situation worsened sharply on Wednesday: 21 people died in the preceding 24 hours alone, taking the state's 2026 monsoon death toll to 31, with more than 5.64 lakh people affected across 12 districts. Sivasagar district recorded 13 of the new deaths, including four women and two children; Charaideo recorded five, Golaghat two, and Jorhat one. The Brahmaputra is flowing above its danger mark at Neamatighat, and tributaries including the Buridihing and Dhansiri rivers are also above danger levels. Authorities are running 273 relief camps housing over 12,000 displaced people, and the India Meteorological Department has forecast more rain in the coming days.
key_points: 21 more people died in Assam in the 24 hours to Tuesday — this year's toll now 31
5.64 lakh (564,000) people affected across 12 districts
The Brahmaputra and several tributaries are now above their danger marks
13 of the new deaths were in Sivasagar district alone, including four women and two children

depth.background: Assam sits on the floodplain of the Brahmaputra, one of the world's largest rivers, and floods every monsoon (India's June-September rainy season) to some degree. This year's monsoon has been unusually intense in the northeast: flash floods and landslides had already killed dozens across Assam, Kashmir and Nagaland over the past few days, with the state's disaster management authority reporting a toll past 10 as of Monday.

thread.previously: We reported Monday that Assam's flood toll had passed 10 with over 3 lakh people affected, alongside separate deadly flooding in Kashmir's Poonch, Rajouri and Doda districts.
thread.changed: The Assam toll alone has now nearly tripled to 31 (21 dead in a single day), with affected people up to 5.64 lakh and the Brahmaputra now above its danger mark in multiple districts — this is a serious escalation, not a continuation of the same level of flooding.

prev_ref.title: Assam's flood toll climbs past 10 as over 3 lakh are hit; Kashmir's Poonch, Rajouri and Doda districts report at least 15 more dead

stories.title: India open their Zimbabwe T20 series Thursday — a fresh audition for Sooryavanshi and a captaincy test for Iyer
stories.what_happened: India begin a three-match T20I series against Zimbabwe on Thursday at the Harare Sports Club, fielding a young squad captained by Shreyas Iyer that includes Abhishek Sharma, Ishan Kishan, Tilak Varma, Shivam Dube and Rinku Singh in the batting, with Ravi Bishnoi and raw pace option Mayank Yadav anchoring the bowling. With Samson out of the squad, Sooryavanshi has a clear run across all three games to press his case for a regular T20I spot. India go in as overwhelming favourites on a Harare pitch that typically favours pace bowlers early before flattening out for batting.
key_points: 1st T20I in Harare on Thursday, India favourites in a 3-match series
Shreyas Iyer captains after series losses in Ireland and England
Sanju Samson left out — opens the door for Vaibhav Sooryavanshi
Ravi Bishnoi and pacer Mayank Yadav lead a young bowling attack

depth.background: India regularly sends a second-string T20I squad on short tours like this one so its top stars can rest or prepare elsewhere, using the games to test fringe players. Shreyas Iyer has been leading these second-string sides but has overseen series defeats in Ireland and England recently, putting some pressure on his captaincy credentials. Vaibhav Sooryavanshi is the teenage batting prodigy who smashed a match-winning 175 in the Under-19 World Cup final in January and is now trying to force his way into the senior T20I picture with wicketkeeper-batter Sanju Samson left out of this squad.

stories.title: India's biggest-ever road InvIT opens for bidding — Cube Highways Trust wants to raise ₹5,000 crore from toll-road investors
stories.what_happened: Cube Highways Trust's initial public offering opened for subscription today, July 22, and closes July 24, with units expected to list on the NSE and BSE on August 3. The trust set a price band of ₹151-152 per unit for the ₹5,000 crore offering, which is entirely an offer-for-sale by existing unit holders — meaning no fresh money goes to the trust itself, only to the investors selling their stakes. As of March 31, 2026, the trust's portfolio spans 27 operational toll roads covering 8,754 lane-kilometres across 12 states and one union territory, with total assets under management of about ₹36,842 crore. Ahead of the public offer, it also raised ₹1,250 crore from strategic investors including a firm called Prazim Trading and Investment.
key_points: Cube Highways Trust's IPO opened today and runs through July 24
Price band set at ₹151-152 per unit; the offer is entirely a sale by existing owners
It owns 27 toll highways spanning 8,754 lane-kilometres across 12 states
Backers include Abu Dhabi's ADIA, Mubadala and Canada's BCI pension fund

depth.background: An InvIT (Infrastructure Investment Trust) is India's version of a REIT (real estate investment trust) but for infrastructure — it lets ordinary investors buy a slice of income-generating assets like toll roads and collect a share of the cash they earn, instead of needing to buy and run a highway themselves. Cube Highways was set up in 2014 to buy and operate toll roads across India and has since built one of the country's largest private road portfolios, backed by large global infrastructure investors.

stories.title: NASA will test SpaceX's and Blue Origin's Moon landers in orbit — before any astronaut tries to actually land in one
stories.what_happened: NASA confirmed that during the Artemis III mission, astronauts aboard Orion will rendezvous and dock separately with test versions — not the final crewed vehicles — of both SpaceX's and Blue Origin's landers in lunar orbit. This lets ground teams and the crew practice the exact maneuvers needed for a real landing without anyone actually setting foot on the Moon yet; that landing is targeted for a later mission in 2028.
key_points: Artemis III, planned for 2027, adds a full dress rehearsal before the real 2028 Moon landing
Orion astronauts will practice docking with prototype landers from BOTH SpaceX and Blue Origin
It's an unusually cautious, redundant approach for a program under pressure to move fast
Follows the successful Artemis II crewed flight around the Moon earlier in 2026

depth.background: NASA's Artemis program is trying to return astronauts to the Moon's surface for the first time since Apollo. Getting there safely requires an Orion capsule (which carries the crew from Earth) to dock in lunar orbit with a separate lander (which actually descends to the surface) — a complex maneuver NASA hasn't attempted since the 1960s and 70s. NASA hired two competing companies, SpaceX (adapting its Starship rocket) and Blue Origin (building "Blue Moon"), to build human landing systems, partly so a delay or failure at one company doesn't strand the whole program.

stories.title: Scientists find a way to revive vancomycin, an antibiotic superbugs had learned to defeat
stories.what_happened: A research team paired vancomycin with a small molecule called pghi-4, which blocks the bacterial enzyme responsible for the resistance. In lab tests, the combination cut the amount of vancomycin needed to kill drug-resistant E. faecium by up to eight times, and the effect held up across multiple real clinical bacterial samples and in infected mice, not just in a test tube. The study was published in the journal Nature Communications.
key_points: New molecule pghi-4 blocks the enzyme bacteria use to resist vancomycin
Combo cut the antibiotic dose needed by up to 8x in lab tests
Worked against real drug-resistant infections from hospital patients
Also reduced bacterial levels in infected mice, not just test tubes

depth.background: Vancomycin is often called an antibiotic 'of last resort' — the drug doctors reach for when other antibiotics have already failed. But a hospital-acquired bacterium called Enterococcus faecium has increasingly evolved resistance to it, leaving doctors with fewer options for some of their sickest patients. Researchers have spent years hunting for a way to restore the drug's power rather than invent a whole new one from scratch, since developing genuinely new antibiotics is slow and expensive.

stories.title: Scientists found a way to make a 70-year-old antibiotic work again against superbugs it had stopped killing
stories.what_happened: Researchers at Scripps Research, publishing in Nature Communications, paired vancomycin with a small molecule called pghi-4 that blocks a bacterial enzyme (called SagA) the resistant bacteria rely on to fend off the drug. In lab tests, this combination restored vancomycin's ability to kill drug-resistant E. faecium strains that had previously survived it. The molecule itself isn't an antibiotic — it's what's called an 'antibiotic adjuvant,' a helper compound that makes an existing drug work again.
key_points: Vancomycin is a 'last resort' antibiotic that some hospital superbugs now resist
Scripps Research scientists found a molecule that disables the bacteria's defense
Paired together, the old drug kills the resistant bacteria again in lab tests
The approach could work as a template for other failing antibiotics too

depth.background: Vancomycin has been one of medicine's most important 'last-line' antibiotics since the 1950s — the drug doctors reach for when other antibiotics have already failed. Over decades, a hospital-acquired bacterium called Enterococcus faecium evolved defenses against it (known as VRE, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus), making some infections nearly untreatable. Antibiotic resistance broadly is one of modern medicine's biggest slow-moving crises: bacteria evolve faster than we invent new drugs.

stories.title: Iran strikes US allies Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan again — claims to hit an Amazon data centre and a US F-15
stories.what_happened: Iran's IRGC (paramilitary Revolutionary Guard) announced fresh missile and drone strikes on US-linked targets across Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan, claiming it destroyed an Amazon Web Services data centre in Bahrain and a US F-15 fighter jet at a Jordanian base — claims that US and host-government officials have not confirmed. Separately, a commercial tanker off Oman was hit in the Strait of Hormuz, forcing its crew to abandon ship. It's the latest escalation after 11 consecutive nights of US airstrikes on Iran.
key_points: Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it fired on US-linked bases and infrastructure in three Gulf countries again
Claims include hitting Amazon's cloud data centre in Bahrain and destroying a US F-15 jet in Jordan — neither confirmed
Comes as the US bombs Iran for an 11th straight night, still without hitting the 'Pickaxe Mountain' nuclear site
A tanker was also struck in the Strait of Hormuz, forcing its crew to abandon ship

depth.background: In February 2026, Israel and the US struck Iran aiming to end its nuclear and missile programs; Iran's Supreme Leader was killed and the war has ground on in waves ever since, with brief ceasefires collapsing repeatedly. Since mid-July, unable to hit Israel or the US mainland directly, Iran has increasingly targeted US military bases and allied infrastructure in nearby Gulf states — Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan — that host American forces.

stories.title: Ukraine's drones hit Russia's biggest online retailer again, this time in the south
stories.what_happened: Ukrainian drones struck two more Wildberries logistics centres — in Krasnodar and Nevinnomyssk in southern Russia — in the early hours of Wednesday, July 22. Krasnodar regional officials said three people were injured at the warehouse there; Stavropol region's governor said five more were hurt at the Nevinnomyssk site. Wildberries confirmed the strikes but said the facilities were purely commercial.
key_points: Drones struck Wildberries warehouses in Krasnodar and Nevinnomyssk early Wednesday
At least 8 people hurt across the two sites, regional officials say
It's the second Wildberries hit in under a week — Kyiv says the sites double as military logistics hubs
Wildberries denies any military use; is Russia's largest e-commerce company

depth.background: Wildberries is essentially Russia's Amazon — a sprawling network of warehouses that ships everything from clothes to electronics across the country. On July 18, Ukrainian drones hit a Wildberries hub in Kotovsk, killing several workers, after President Zelensky said the facility was secretly being used to store navigation equipment and drone components for the Russian military. Moscow denied it. Ukraine has increasingly targeted logistics and industrial sites deep inside Russia, arguing that modern militaries can't fight without civilian supply chains feeding them.

stories.title: Nearly 1 in 4 US workers are stuck in jobs they hate just to keep their health insurance
stories.what_happened: A new survey from the West Health–Gallup Center on Healthcare in America finds that 24% of US employees — roughly 23 million adults — say they are staying in a job they would otherwise leave purely to hold on to employer health insurance, up from 16% in 2021. Among workers with a chronic health condition, that figure jumps to 41%. Ellyn Maese, the Center's research director, called the situation 'crazy' for people who want to leave but feel trapped.
key_points: 24% of US workers — about 23 million people — say they're staying in a job just to keep their health coverage
That's up from 16% in 2021; workers with chronic illness are hit hardest at 41%
The jump follows the expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies at the end of 2025
Economists call this 'job lock' — it freezes people out of new jobs, startups, and early retirement

depth.background: In the US, most working-age adults get health insurance through their employer rather than the government — a quirk left over from WWII-era wage controls, when tax-free health benefits became a way for companies to compete for workers without breaking pay caps. The Affordable Care Act (ACA, 'Obamacare') created an alternative: marketplaces where people can buy their own individual plans. In 2021, Congress temporarily made those marketplace plans much cheaper with enhanced subsidies, which gave people real freedom to quit a job without losing affordable coverage.

stories.title: US carries out an 11th straight night of strikes on Iran as Trump threatens to bomb a power plant for every ship Iran hits
stories.what_happened: CENTCOM (the US military's Middle East command) carried out its 11th straight night of strikes on Iran late Tuesday, hitting military operations centers, aircraft hangars, drone-storage sites and logistics infrastructure meant to degrade Iran's ability to threaten shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's health ministry says the campaign has now killed 50 civilians and wounded 500. The Pentagon separately confirmed a 4th American service member has died in the conflict, with US wounded now well over 500. Trump added a new threat overnight: for every commercial ship Iran hits, the US will bomb an Iranian power plant.
key_points: US warplanes and ships struck Iranian military sites for about 75 minutes — the 11th consecutive night of strikes
Trump says he'll hit an Iranian power plant every time Iran attacks a commercial ship
Iran's health ministry says 50 civilians have been killed and 500 wounded by the US strikes so far
A 4th American service member's death in the war has now been confirmed, with over 500 US troops wounded

depth.background: The US and Israel opened this war on Iran back in late February 2026, and Washington has since run a nightly bombing campaign aimed at Iran's military, naval and nuclear-linked sites. A ceasefire announced in mid-June collapsed within weeks after Iran-linked strikes on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway that a fifth of the world's oil passes through. Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth told Congress this week the war has already cost $37.5 billion, and yesterday Trump threatened to hit Iran's underground 'Pickaxe Mountain' site after Tehran struck three more Gulf allies (Bahrain, Kuwait and Jordan).

thread.previously: Yesterday, Trump threatened to hit Iran's underground 'Pickaxe Mountain' site after Iran struck three more Gulf allies (Bahrain, Kuwait, Jordan), as the Pentagon told Congress the war had already cost $37.5 billion.
thread.changed: The US has now completed an 11th consecutive night of strikes, Iran's health ministry has given its first civilian casualty count (50 killed, 500 wounded), a 4th American service member's death was confirmed, and Trump has issued a new, more specific threat: a power plant hit for every ship Iran attacks.

stories.title: NYC Mayor Mamdani says the city can't arrest Netanyahu — but says Washington should
stories.what_happened: Mamdani said late Tuesday that his administration reviewed every option and concluded New York City itself has no independent legal authority to enforce the ICC's warrant. In a video message, he called Netanyahu a 'war criminal,' said he is not welcome in New York, and called on the US federal government to join the ICC and execute the warrant on Washington's behalf. President Trump has already said Netanyahu will not be arrested when he visits the city in September, effectively closing that door at the federal level too.
key_points: Mamdani: NYC lacks legal authority to execute the ICC's Netanyahu arrest warrant
He calls Netanyahu a 'war criminal' and says he's not welcome in the city
He urges the federal government to join the ICC and act on the warrant instead
Trump has separately said Netanyahu 'will not be arrested' if he visits NYC in September

depth.background: In November 2024, the International Criminal Court (ICC) — a permanent tribunal in The Hague that prosecutes war crimes and crimes against humanity when national courts won't — issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, accusing him of using starvation as a weapon of war and directing attacks on civilians in Gaza. The US and Israel don't recognize the ICC's jurisdiction over them, so the warrant has never been enforced. Zohran Mamdani, a vocal critic of Israel's Gaza campaign, became New York City's mayor this year and has repeatedly said he'd have Netanyahu arrested if he set foot in the city.

stories.title: Drone strike sets fire near Russia's largest steel plant in Lipetsk
stories.what_happened: Overnight on July 21–22, explosions and a large fire (reported to cover roughly 2,500 square metres) broke out in Lipetsk near the Novolipetsk Metallurgical Plant (NLMK), one of Russia's biggest steelworks, and near a power station (CHPP-2). Russian regional governor Igor Artamonov confirmed a fire at industrial facilities but said the cause was still under investigation and did not confirm an attack. Ukrainian officials have not publicly claimed it.
key_points: Overnight explosions and a fire broke out near NLMK's Lipetsk steelworks
NLMK makes ~18% of Russia's total steel and 14 million tonnes a year
A power plant (CHPP-2) in the same area also caught fire
Russian officials confirm the fire but not the cause; Kyiv hasn't commented

depth.background: Since the full-scale war began, Ukraine has increasingly used long-range drones to hit Russian industrial and energy sites far from the front line — refineries, power stations, and factories that help fund or supply the Russian war effort — rather than only battlefield targets. Lipetsk, about 400km south of Moscow, is normally well outside the usual strike zone, making a hit there notable.

stories.title: The US launches its 11th straight night of strikes on Iran — and still hasn't hit Pickaxe Mountain
stories.what_happened: US Central Command said it launched an 11th straight night of strikes on Iranian military targets late Tuesday, extending a bombing campaign that has now run for over a week and a half without a resolution. Despite Trump's public threat, the US has not yet struck Pickaxe Mountain itself. War Secretary Pete Hegseth told the Senate this week the campaign has already cost $37.5 billion, with the administration asking Congress for $67 billion more. Iran's military command warned that any strike on its nuclear or other sensitive sites would be treated as an escalation of the war across the region.
key_points: CENTCOM confirmed an 11th consecutive night of US strikes on Iranian military targets
Trump repeated his threat to hit the fortified 'Pickaxe Mountain' site but gave no timing
Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya command warned a strike on nuclear sites would expand the war
US officials say Trump faces a fork: a new 10-day ceasefire, or a bigger joint campaign with Israel

depth.background: The US and Iran have been trading direct strikes for over a week and a half after the fight over the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway that carries roughly a fifth of the world's oil — reignited. On Tuesday, July 21, Trump named Pickaxe Mountain, a fortified underground tunnel complex near Iran's Natanz nuclear site, as a target 'pretty soon.' Iran responded the same day by striking Kuwait, Bahrain and Jordan — three US-allied Gulf states hosting American bases — rather than absorbing the threat quietly.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported Trump named Pickaxe Mountain as a target 'pretty soon, and very heavily' for the first time, on the same day Iran struck Kuwait, Bahrain and Jordan in retaliation — the 10th straight night of US strikes.
thread.changed: The US has now extended the campaign to an 11th straight night without actually striking Pickaxe Mountain, and officials have laid out the two broad paths Trump is weighing next: a new ceasefire or a bigger joint campaign with Israel.

stories.title: President Murmu makes history as first Indian head of state to visit North Macedonia, pushes to double trade
stories.what_happened: President Murmu held bilateral talks with North Macedonia's president and prime minister, addressed the country's Assembly (parliament), and spoke at the India-North Macedonia Business Forum, where she urged both countries to aim to double their bilateral trade volume by the end of the decade and to diversify trade into new sectors.
key_points: Murmu addressed the India-North Macedonia Business Forum in Skopje
She called for doubling bilateral trade by the end of the decade
Part of a three-nation Europe tour: Moldova, North Macedonia, Romania
Focus areas flagged: agriculture, pharma, IT and tourism

depth.background: India has been working to deepen ties with Central and Eastern Europe as it looks to diversify trade partnerships beyond its traditional markets. President Droupadi Murmu began a tour of Moldova, North Macedonia and Romania on July 19 — her stop in North Macedonia is the first-ever visit by an Indian head of state to the country.

stories.title: Sri Lanka captain Kusal Mendis ruled out of LPL with a hamstring injury, clouding India Test series
stories.what_happened: Mendis suffered a right hamstring injury while attempting a run during Colombo Kaps' LPL match against Kandy Royals on July 19. He tried to continue but was forced to retire hurt after a medical assessment, two overs into the run chase. He has now been ruled out of the remainder of the 2026 LPL, with Kamindu Mendis stepping in as Kaps captain, while Kusal begins a rehabilitation program at Sri Lanka's National High Performance Centre.
key_points: Mendis hurt his hamstring running between the wickets against Kandy Royals on July 19
Ruled out of the rest of Lanka Premier League 2026; Kamindu Mendis takes over as Colombo Kaps captain
Raises doubts over his fitness for Sri Lanka's two-Test series against India starting August 15
He's now back at the National High Performance Centre beginning rehab

depth.background: Kusal Mendis is Sri Lanka's first-choice wicketkeeper-batter and was captaining Colombo Kaps in this year's Lanka Premier League (LPL), the country's domestic T20 franchise tournament. He's also a key part of Sri Lanka's squad for a high-profile two-Test home series against India starting August 15 — a series that matters a lot for Sri Lankan cricket given how rarely they get to host India in Tests.

stories.title: Babar Azam marks his return as Pakistan's Test captain with a century, as Pakistan flatten West Indies in a one-sided warm-up draw
stories.what_happened: Batting first at the Brian Lara Cricket Academy, Pakistan declared their first innings on 455-4 after 136.5 overs. Babar Azam made a fluent 100 off 152 balls, Azan Awais ground out a patient 100 from 241 deliveries, and Shan Masood added a brisk 70. In reply, West Indies Select XI were bowled out for 279, with fast bowler Mohammad Ali claiming 5-37. Pakistan then reached 219-4 in their second innings before both sides agreed to end the four-day match as a draw, with Pakistan 395 runs ahead overall.
key_points: Babar Azam (100) and Azan Awais (100) both scored centuries as Pakistan piled up 455-4 declared
Mohammad Ali ran through West Indies Select XI with 5-37
Pakistan finished 395 runs ahead when the four-day warm-up match was drawn
It sets up the first-ever men's Test at Trinidad's Brian Lara Cricket Academy from July 25

depth.background: Babar Azam, one of the most prolific batters of his generation, was removed as Pakistan's Test captain amid a turbulent stretch for the team before being reinstated to lead the side again. This warm-up match against a West Indies Select XI was his first opportunity to show his form with the bat since returning to the captaincy, ahead of a two-match Test series against West Indies that carries real Test Championship points.

stories.title: A 20-year-old Bulgarian is running away with Formula 2 — and F1 teams are taking notice
stories.what_happened: At the Spa-Francorchamps round, Rafael Camara won Sunday's feature race, but championship leader Nikola Tsolov of the Red Bull junior programme extended his overall points lead regardless, moving to 161 points. Gabriele Mini (Alpine Academy) sits second on 134, Camara third on 125, and Alex Dunne (also Alpine) fourth on 108. Tsolov has already taken six wins this season, including three consecutive victories — a feat matched in F2's modern era only by Davide Valsecchi during the old GP2 series.
key_points: Red Bull junior Nikola Tsolov leads F2 with 161 points after Spa, well clear of the field
He's already won 6 races this season, including 3 in a row — a modern F2 record
Alpine's Gabriele Mini (134) and Alex Dunne (108), and Ferrari's Rafael Camara (125), trail him
A strong F2 season is the clearest ticket to a future Formula 1 seat

depth.background: Formula 2 is the direct feeder series to Formula 1 — nearly every current F1 driver came through it. Teams' junior driver academies (Red Bull, Ferrari, Alpine, McLaren and others) sponsor promising young drivers through F2, using their results to decide who gets promoted, who gets F1 practice sessions, and who gets dropped. With multiple F1 teams' driver line-ups still unsettled for 2027, this year's F2 title fight is being watched unusually closely.

stories.title: OpenAI commits up to $30 billion to a new 'Project Camellia' data center in Georgia, and launches its first enterprise AI agent platform
stories.what_happened: OpenAI announced 'Project Camellia,' a data center campus in Effingham County, Georgia, that will eventually draw 3.2 gigawatts of power — roughly enough to power a couple of million homes. OpenAI has committed $20 billion so far, with the fully built-out site likely to cost more than $30 billion; construction is planned in phases from 2028 to 2032, and the company is still seeking partners to help finance and build it. Alongside the infrastructure news, OpenAI officially launched 'Presence,' an enterprise AI agent platform designed to plug its models directly into a company's internal data, policies, and workflows. OpenAI also pledged $80 million in community benefits — covering education, public safety, healthcare, workforce development, and small-business support — to address local opposition to the project.
key_points: New 3.2-gigawatt data center campus planned for Effingham County, Georgia
$20B committed so far; full build likely tops $30B, spanning 1,400 acres
Power to arrive in phases from 2028 through 2032
OpenAI also launched 'Presence,' its enterprise AI agent platform

depth.background: Training and running today's most powerful AI models takes enormous amounts of computing power and, in turn, electricity — far more than existing data centers were built to supply. OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, has been racing rivals like Google and Anthropic to lock down that future power and computing capacity years in advance, striking massive infrastructure deals across the US. Communities near these projects have increasingly pushed back over the land, water, and electricity such mega-projects consume.

stories.title: Yemen's Houthis strike two Saudi oil tankers, opening a dangerous new front alongside the collapsing Iran ceasefire
stories.what_happened: The Houthis said Wednesday they had targeted two Saudi oil tankers, named Encelia and Layla, with drones and missiles, accusing them of breaking the naval blockade the group announced days earlier. Saudi Arabia responded by suspending some oil shipments through the Red Sea. The Institute for the Study of War reported that at least seven vessels had already changed course to avoid the Bab el-Mandeb Strait because of the blockade threat. On Thursday, President Trump said the United States would hold Iran responsible for any further Houthi attacks, tying the group's actions directly to Tehran.
key_points: Houthis say they hit tankers Encelia and Layla with drones and missiles
Attack is the first since their new naval blockade of Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia has suspended some oil shipments through the Red Sea
Trump says the US will hold Iran responsible for future Houthi attacks

depth.background: The Houthis are an Iran-backed armed group that controls most of Yemen and has fought a long civil war against the internationally recognized Yemeni government, which Saudi Arabia has backed for a decade. On Monday this week the Houthis announced a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, a major escalation that followed weeks of rising US-Iran tension after a ceasefire in their direct conflict began breaking down. The Red Sea and its narrow southern entrance, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, are one of the world's busiest shipping corridors, carrying a huge share of the oil and cargo that moves between Asia, Europe, and the Americas.

stories.title: Jaishankar tells China's Wang Yi that fixing trade imbalance and market access is key to normalizing ties, as the two meet on the sidelines in Manila
stories.what_happened: India's External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar met his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi on the sidelines of a regional foreign ministers' gathering in Manila on Wednesday. Jaishankar said the two countries needed to address issues like fair market access and the trade balance as part of repairing relations, and reiterated that peace and tranquility along the disputed border remains a prerequisite for any return to normal ties.
key_points: Jaishankar and Wang Yi met on the sidelines of a regional ASEAN gathering in Manila
Jaishankar raised fair market access and India's trade imbalance with China
He repeated that border peace remains a 'prerequisite' for normal ties
Comes as India and China have been slowly easing tensions since their 2020 border clash

depth.background: India and China fought a deadly military clash along their disputed Himalayan border in Galwan Valley in 2020, which froze high-level ties and trade cooperation for years. Since late 2024 the two sides have been cautiously de-escalating — restoring some direct flights and border trade — but deep mistrust remains, and India runs a large and growing trade deficit with China, importing far more (mostly electronics and machinery components) than it exports.

stories.title: Webb telescope finds a third giant planet hiding inside a nearby star's dust disk — the first exoplanet confirmed by its atmosphere alone
stories.what_happened: Using the James Webb Space Telescope together with the Very Large Telescope, astronomers at UC San Diego and Edinburgh confirmed a third giant planet, Beta Pictoris d, hiding inside the star's dust disk. Instead of photographing it directly, they detected it through atmospheric spectroscopy — reading the chemical fingerprint of starlight filtering through its atmosphere, finding carbon monoxide, water vapor and methane.
key_points: Beta Pictoris d found hidden inside a bright dust disk studied for decades
Confirmed via atmospheric gases (carbon monoxide, water, methane) — not a photo
System now has 3 known giant planets; d has the widest orbit
Star is 63 light-years away and only about 23 million years old

depth.background: Beta Pictoris is one of astronomy's most-studied young star systems — its first known planet, Beta Pictoris b, was among the very first exoplanets ever directly photographed. Astronomers already knew of a second planet, c. The system is surrounded by a huge disk of leftover dust and debris, the same kind of material planets form from, which partly blocks the view of anything orbiting inside it.

stories.title: Trump vows to bomb an Iranian bridge or power plant every time Iran fires on a ship in the Strait of Hormuz
stories.what_happened: President Trump said this week that from now on, every time Iran fires a missile, rocket, drone or any other weapon at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, the US will destroy one Iranian bridge or power plant in response — explicitly including targets in or next to Tehran. A senior Iranian official replied that Tehran would in turn strike 'infrastructure and bridges across the region.'
key_points: Trump: one Iranian bridge or power plant destroyed per ship attack in Hormuz
Threat explicitly includes targets 'in the Capital City of Tehran'
Iran responds: it will hit 'infrastructure and bridges across the region'
Comes as the collapsed ceasefire pushes oil toward $95 a barrel

depth.background: The US and Iran have been fighting a war since a ceasefire collapsed a few weeks ago, with Iran firing on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly a fifth of the world's oil physically passes through every day. Trump has threatened Iran's power plants before; this is different because it's a standing, automatic retaliation rule rather than a one-off warning.

stories.title: Zomato and Blinkit's parent Eternal posts profit up 268%, as its 10-minute grocery arm turns profitable for the first time
stories.what_happened: Eternal reported Q1 FY27 (April-June 2026) consolidated net profit of ₹92 crore, up 268% from ₹25 crore a year earlier, on revenue that grew 182% to ₹20,211 crore. Blinkit alone brought in ₹15,664 crore of that revenue — more than six times what it made a year ago — and swung from a ₹162 crore loss to a ₹102 crore profit at the adjusted-EBITDA level, adding 899 new dark stores over the year. Core Zomato food delivery grew a steadier 37% to ₹3,100 crore.
key_points: Consolidated net profit up 268% YoY to ₹92 crore
Revenue up 182% YoY to ₹20,211 crore
Blinkit (quick commerce) swung from an EBITDA loss to a ₹102 crore profit
Blinkit is now Eternal's single biggest revenue source, ahead of food delivery

depth.background: Eternal is the parent company of Zomato (food delivery) and Blinkit (10-minute grocery delivery) — renamed from Zomato Limited last year. Blinkit and India's other 'quick commerce' apps have spent heavily building dark stores (small local warehouses) to promise 10-minute deliveries, burning cash for years to grab market share ahead of rivals like Swiggy's Instamart and Zepto.

stories.title: David Warner pleads guilty to drink-driving, with sentencing due next month and his Sydney Thunder captaincy under scrutiny
stories.what_happened: Warner's lawyer entered a guilty plea on his behalf at Waverley Local Court this week to a mid-range drink-driving charge. Police had stopped him on Easter Sunday, and a breath test at Maroubra Police Station recorded a blood alcohol reading of 0.104 — more than double the legal limit. His lawyer says Warner is remorseful and will seek leniency; sentencing is set for August 18.
key_points: Guilty plea entered via lawyer at Waverley Local Court, Sydney
Blood alcohol reading of 0.104 — more than double the legal limit
Incident happened on Easter Sunday; sentencing set for August 18
Cricket NSW says it takes the matter 'very seriously'

depth.background: David Warner is a former Australia Test and ODI opener, one of the country's most recognisable cricketers, who now captains the Sydney Thunder in Australia's Big Bash T20 league. He was charged in April after being stopped by police in Sydney's eastern suburbs.

stories.title: Alphabet's cloud business grew 82% — but Wall Street punished the stock anyway, over a $205 billion spending plan
stories.what_happened: Alphabet reported Q2 2026 earnings that beat Wall Street's revenue and profit estimates, driven by Google Cloud revenue soaring 82% year-on-year to $24.8 billion. But the company also raised its full-year 2026 capital-expenditure forecast to a range of $195-205 billion, up from the $180-190 billion it had guided just one quarter earlier. Investors sent the stock down roughly 3-6% in after-hours trading, focused less on the earnings beat and more on how much more Alphabet plans to spend before that spending turns into durable profit.
key_points: Google Cloud revenue jumped 82% to $24.8 billion in Q2
Alphabet raised 2026 capex guidance to as much as $205 billion
Shares fell around 3-6% in after-hours trading despite beating estimates
Investors are worried about how fast AI spending is outrunning AI profits

depth.background: Alphabet is Google's parent company, and its cloud division rents out computing power and AI tools to other businesses — it's become one of the clearest ways to measure real-world demand for AI. 'Capex' (capital expenditure) is money a company spends building long-life assets like data centers and chips; it shows up on the books for years, unlike a salary or a marketing budget. Alphabet, along with Microsoft, Amazon and Meta, has spent 2025 and 2026 in an unprecedented arms race to build AI data centers, each raising its spending forecasts every quarter.

stories.title: Delhi High Court orders activist Sonam Wangchuk moved to a private hospital as his hunger-strike health crisis deepens
stories.what_happened: The Delhi High Court ordered that Wangchuk be shifted from the government-run Safdarjung Hospital to Medanta, a private hospital, after government and private doctors agreed he needed continuous medical monitoring. Officials told the court his prolonged fasting had caused ketosis (a state where the body burns fat for fuel because it lacks carbohydrates, which can be dangerous if extended) and other complications.
key_points: Court cites doctors' consensus that Wangchuk needs continuous monitoring
He has been on an extended hunger strike demanding the education minister's resignation
Government doctors say prolonged fasting has caused ketosis and other complications
His wife had petitioned the court days earlier after an initial refusal

depth.background: Sonam Wangchuk is a Ladakh-based education reformer and climate activist who has spent years campaigning for statehood and constitutional protections for Ladakh, and more recently for accountability over a NEET-UG (India's medical college entrance exam) paper-leak scandal. He was taken from a protest at Jantar Mantar in Delhi and admitted to Safdarjung Hospital, a government facility, while on an indefinite hunger strike demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. His wife, Gitanjali Angmo, first asked the Delhi High Court to move him to a private hospital of the family's choice; the court initially declined but reversed course days later.

stories.title: Dr Reddy's profit crashes 69% after a diabetes-drug manufacturing problem and a lost US deal
stories.what_happened: For the April-June quarter, Dr Reddy's net profit fell 69% year-on-year to roughly ₹444 crore, while revenue slipped 5.5% to ₹8,070.5 crore. North America sales — its biggest market — fell over 35% to ₹2,204.8 crore, largely because the lenalidomide deal ended. Separately, a quality problem with the active ingredient in its generic semaglutide forced the company to halt new production batches and set aside a ₹240 crore provision; supplies will stay disrupted in India and Canada until at least late October. Higher freight and solvent costs, linked partly to the ongoing Middle East conflict, added further pressure. The stock fell over 4% on the news as brokerages cut their earnings estimates.
key_points: Net profit fell 69% year-on-year to about ₹444 crore in the June quarter
Revenue dipped 5.5% to ₹8,070 crore
A quality issue forced Dr Reddy's to set aside ₹240 crore for its generic semaglutide (a diabetes/weight-loss drug)
It also lost a lucrative 4-year deal to sell generic lenalidomide, a cancer drug, in the US

depth.background: Dr Reddy's Laboratories is one of India's largest generic-drug makers, selling copies of branded medicines once their patents expire — often in the US, its biggest market. A big part of its recent profit came from a temporary, exclusive deal to sell a generic version of lenalidomide (a cancer treatment) in the US; that agreement ended in January 2026, so the earnings boost it provided is now gone. The company was also ramping up sales of a generic version of semaglutide (the active ingredient in drugs like Ozempic/Wegovy, used for diabetes and weight loss), one of the hottest drug categories in the world right now.

stories.title: Bira 91's founder gives up his stake and exits the board after a two-year fight with lenders
stories.what_happened: Ankur Jain, founder of B9 Beverages (Bira 91's parent company), has stepped down from the board and surrendered a 17.8% ownership stake as part of a settlement with lenders and institutional shareholders. Both sides agreed to withdraw litigation and claims against each other, and Jain's personal guarantees on the company's corporate loans will be released. The company says it will now pursue an out-of-court financial restructuring and seek fresh capital to stabilize operations.
key_points: Ankur Jain surrenders a 17.8% stake in B9 Beverages, Bira 91's parent, and steps down from the board
The settlement ends a roughly two-year dispute with lenders and institutional shareholders
B9 Beverages lost ₹748.8 crore on ₹638.5 crore of revenue in FY24
The company will now pursue an out-of-court restructuring and try to raise fresh capital

depth.background: Bira 91 grew into one of India's best-known craft beer brands through aggressive, investor-funded expansion, backed at various points by Sequoia and Japan's Kirin Holdings (which has separately been reported to be exploring an exit). That growth-first strategy left the company burning cash faster than it could generate it, and lenders and investors had spent roughly two years pushing for a change in leadership and governance.

stories.title: Carlos Sainz sets Williams a deadline to prove it deserves him for 2027
stories.what_happened: Amid growing speculation about his future, Carlos Sainz has reportedly told Williams he wants to see concrete progress before deciding whether to stay for 2027 — with reports pointing to the Azerbaijan Grand Prix in Baku (September 24-26), where Williams plans to bring a significant car upgrade, as his informal deadline. Team principal James Vowles says Sainz genuinely wants to end his career at Williams, but acknowledged nothing is guaranteed until a contract is signed.
key_points: Sainz is out of contract at Williams at the end of 2026, with no extension signed
Reports say he's given Williams until the Azerbaijan GP in Baku (September) to show its upgrades work
Audi's Nico Hulkenberg has ruled himself out of a swap, leaving Alpine as reportedly Sainz's main alternative
Williams boss James Vowles says Sainz wants to retire at Williams — but 'you can never be sure'

depth.background: Williams bet heavily on F1's new 2026 technical rules hoping to return to the front of the grid, but has instead fielded an uncompetitive, overweight car all season. Sainz joined the team in 2025 specifically to help lead that rebuild, after leaving Ferrari.

stories.title: Gaza's 'ceasefire' has killed 1,180 people since it was signed — and Israel now holds 70% of the strip
stories.what_happened: Gaza's Health Ministry said this week that Israeli strikes have killed 1,180 Palestinians since the ceasefire was signed, including 11 in the 24 hours before the report — among them a family of six killed in a strike on a Gaza City apartment. Separately, monitors and local reporting describe Israeli forces steadily expanding their footprint, now controlling around 70% of Gaza rather than the 53% laid out in the agreement.
key_points: Gaza's Health Ministry says 1,180 Palestinians have died in Israeli strikes since the October 2025 ceasefire took effect
Israel's military now controls roughly 70% of Gaza's territory, versus the 53% the ceasefire deal assigned it
A funeral strike and a family of six killed in an apartment strike are among the latest incidents
Neither side has formally declared the truce dead — but the death toll keeps climbing

depth.background: The US-brokered ceasefire between Israel and Hamas took effect in October 2025, ending nearly two years of war that killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and devastated Gaza. The deal was meant to halt fighting, let aid in, and set a path toward a longer-term settlement, with Israeli forces pulling back to an agreed 53% of Gaza's territory while the rest stayed under a transitional arrangement.

stories.title: Lalit Modi wins his 16-year IPL legal battle — and plans to finally return to India
stories.what_happened: The Appellate Tribunal under SAFEMA (the law governing forfeiture of illegally-acquired foreign exchange property) ruled that the foreign payments related to IPL 2009 were ordinary 'current account' transactions — routine payments for services — rather than the restricted 'capital account' transfers the Enforcement Directorate had alleged. The tribunal also found Modi personally wasn't responsible for the BCCI's compliance obligations, and set aside the penalties against him. Modi, in a statement from London, said he's now looking at returning to India for the first time in 16 years.
key_points: A SAFEMA appellate tribunal set aside most penalties against Modi from the 2009 IPL-in-South-Africa case
The tribunal ruled the disputed foreign transfers were routine payments, not the illegal capital transfers he was accused of
Modi says he's 'looking forward to' returning to India after 16 years of self-exile in London
He was the IPL's founding chairman before being banned for life by the BCCI in 2010

depth.background: Lalit Modi founded and ran the Indian Premier League (IPL) — cricket's biggest T20 league — from 2008 until he was suspended and later banned for life by the BCCI (India's cricket board) in 2010, amid allegations of financial irregularities. One case centered on the 2009 IPL season, which had to be moved out of India to South Africa because of security concerns around that year's general election; the government's Enforcement Directorate alleged the BCCI sent nearly $50 million overseas for that tournament without the required central bank approval, a violation of India's foreign exchange law (FEMA). Modi has lived in London ever since, fighting the case.

stories.title: Mercedes sets a team-orders rule for Antonelli and Russell — but only if a rival is closing in
stories.what_happened: At the Spanish Grand Prix in Barcelona, Russell and Antonelli spent six laps racing wheel-to-wheel for the lead — a battle that let Hamilton close a 13-second gap on Antonelli over that stretch. Wolff has now set a clear boundary: Mercedes won't order Russell to simply hand position to Antonelli just because of the points table, but if a rival team is genuinely closing in and threatening to profit from an internal Mercedes fight, team orders will apply.
key_points: Team boss Toto Wolff won't yet make Russell a No. 2 driver despite Antonelli's championship lead
But both drivers agree team orders will kick in if a rival is genuinely threatening to steal points
The rule follows a costly Barcelona incident where the teammates' fight let Hamilton close the gap
Antonelli leads Russell by 50 points and Hamilton by 45 heading into Hungary

depth.background: Kimi Antonelli, in his first full F1 season with Mercedes, has taken over as championship leader ahead of veteran teammate George Russell, with Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton also in the title fight after his high-profile move from Mercedes. Team orders — when a team instructs one driver to yield position to a teammate, usually to protect a championship lead or race result — are a routine but sensitive tool in F1, since fans and drivers alike want to see fair, open racing between teammates.

stories.title: Oil jumps toward $95 a barrel as the US-Iran ceasefire fully collapses and Rubio calls Iran 'not serious' about peace
stories.what_happened: US Central Command carried out an 11th consecutive night of strikes on Iran this week, as Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared Tehran 'not serious' about diplomatic talks — a notable hardening from his comments just a day earlier that the US remained open to a deal. Brent crude jumped nearly 5% toward $95 a barrel and US pump prices extended their climb above $4 a gallon as traders priced in a ceasefire that looks fully collapsed rather than merely strained.
key_points: Brent crude rose as much as 4.9% toward $95/barrel, a nearly six-week high
US strikes hit Iran for an 11th straight night as diplomacy stalls
Rubio says Tehran is 'not serious' about talks — a sharp reversal from his stance a day earlier
US pump prices are climbing again, extending their rise above $4/gallon

depth.background: The US and Iran agreed a ceasefire in April after a direct war, and signed a memorandum of understanding in June meant to lead to a lasting peace. That truce has repeatedly broken down since, with both sides trading strikes — the pattern our earlier coverage has tracked through Iran's tanker attacks and Trump's retaliation threats.

thread.previously: We reported Rubio saying the US remained open to an Iran deal, while warning that Iran's demand over a Hormuz shipping toll could 'threaten the world economy.'
thread.changed: Rubio has now hardened his tone, calling Iran 'not serious' about talks, as US strikes reach an 11th straight night and oil jumps toward $95 a barrel — the ceasefire looks fully collapsed rather than just strained.

prev_ref.title: Rubio says the US is open to an Iran deal, but warns Iran's Hormuz toll demand would 'threaten the world economy'

stories.title: Zelenskyy fires Ukraine's top general and defense minister in one week, installs a younger war cabinet
stories.what_happened: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy fired commander-in-chief Oleksandr Syrskyi on Wednesday and replaced him with 43-year-old General Mykhailo Drapatyi, described as part of a newer generation of commanders. The move came days after Zelenskyy removed defense minister and close ally Mykhailo Fedorov, whose public clashes with Syrskyi over military strategy triggered rare street protests in Kyiv. Drapatyi said the military would 'continue and intensify offensive operations in all domains.'
key_points: Zelenskyy sacked army chief Oleksandr Syrskyi, days after removing defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov
43-year-old Mykhailo Drapatyi named the new commander-in-chief
Move followed a week of rare wartime protests in Kyiv over war strategy
Drapatyi has pledged to 'intensify offensive operations in all domains'

depth.background: Ukraine has fought Russia's full-scale invasion since February 2022. Zelenskyy had largely kept the same senior military and political team in place for most of the war, valuing continuity. Syrskyi, a Soviet-trained general nicknamed 'the Butcher' by critics for costly battlefield decisions, had led Ukraine's armed forces since February 2024. Frustration over his strategy — and over the war effort's broader direction — had been building for months among soldiers and the public.

stories.title: BCCI bans no-ball offenders for the rest of the match and axes forfeiture in new domestic playing rules
stories.what_happened: The BCCI announced playing-condition changes for India's 2026-27 domestic season. The headline change: a bowler found by umpires to have deliberately bowled a no-ball — overstepping or not releasing the ball properly — is now suspended for the remainder of the match, up from just the rest of that innings. The board also scrapped the option for teams to declare or forfeit the final innings of a red-ball match, redefined what counts as an 'overthrow,' and eased wicketkeeper glove-positioning rules.
key_points: A bowler ruled to have deliberately bowled a no-ball is now suspended for the rest of the match, not just the innings
Teams can no longer declare or forfeit an innings to manufacture a red-ball result
Wicketkeepers only need gloves behind the stumps at the moment of delivery, not through the run-up
New rules apply from next month's Duleep Trophy, the start of the 2026-27 domestic season

depth.background: Domestic cricket boards set their own playing conditions and often trial changes before they're proposed as international law through the MCC, cricket's rule-making body. India's BCCI runs the world's largest domestic cricket program, and its rule changes often shape the global conversation about the sport's laws.

stories.title: Verstappen can now trigger an exit clause to leave Red Bull for 2027 — and rival drivers are already calling
stories.what_happened: A clause in Verstappen's Red Bull contract has been triggered because he finished the Belgian Grand Prix outside the top two in the championship standings, the threshold written into his deal. That gives him the option — not the obligation — to leave for another team in 2027. Red Bull principal Laurent Mekies confirmed this week that 'many good drivers' have already been in touch about a potential Red Bull seat, while saying he remains confident Verstappen will stay.
key_points: A performance clause in Verstappen's contract activates because he wasn't top-2 in the standings after Belgium
Red Bull boss Laurent Mekies admits 'many good drivers' are already enquiring about a seat
17 F1 driver contracts expire after this season, setting up a chaotic 2027 market
Verstappen's camp says a decision could come before the summer break

depth.background: Max Verstappen has won four world championships with Red Bull, but the team's form has dipped this season against Mercedes and Ferrari. Like most top F1 drivers, his contract — running on paper through 2028 — contains performance-linked clauses letting him leave early if results fall short of a set bar, a common way both driver and team hedge against decline.

stories.title: A US judge sets a June 2027 trial date for Venezuela's ousted leader Maduro
stories.what_happened: At a hearing in Manhattan federal court on Wednesday, Judge Alvin Hellerstein set June 1, 2027 as the trial date for Maduro and Flores. He also scheduled a separate hearing for November on a defense motion to dismiss the case on grounds of sovereign immunity — the argument that Maduro cannot be prosecuted in a US court because he was acting as the head of a sovereign nation.
key_points: Judge sets June 1, 2027 as the trial date for Maduro and wife Cilia Flores
Both face US drug-trafficking, kidnapping and murder charges
Maduro was captured by US special forces in Caracas in January
Defense will argue in November that Maduro is immune from US prosecution

depth.background: In January, US special forces carried out an overnight raid on Nicolás Maduro's home in Caracas and flew him and his wife, Cilia Flores, to the United States, ending his rule of Venezuela. Since then the country has been run by his former vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has built closer ties with the Trump administration. US federal prosecutors indicted Maduro and Flores in New York, accusing them of conspiring with drug cartels to move thousands of tons of cocaine into the US. Both pleaded not guilty and, through their lawyers, have disputed the very legitimacy of trying a former head of state in a US court.

stories.title: A Chinese coast guard attack injures a Philippine sailor near a disputed reef — Manila summons Beijing's envoy as the US, Japan and Australia rally behind it
stories.what_happened: Chinese coast guard personnel clashed with Philippine Navy personnel at Ayungin Shoal on Monday, July 20, injuring at least one Filipino sailor. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. summoned China's ambassador, Jing Quan, to the presidential palace on Wednesday to protest the incident; China, in turn, summoned the Philippine ambassador in Beijing. Days later, Marcos met US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who underscored Washington's commitment to freedom of navigation in the sea, and separately met with Japanese and Australian counterparts.
key_points: Chinese coast guard personnel injured a Philippine Navy sailor at Ayungin Shoal on Monday
Marcos summoned China's ambassador; Beijing summoned the Philippine envoy right back
It's the 10th anniversary of the 2016 international ruling that favored the Philippines over China here
US Secretary of State Rubio met Marcos this week to reaffirm support for freedom of navigation

depth.background: Ayungin Shoal (also called Second Thomas Shoal) is a reef in the South China Sea inside the Philippines' internationally recognized economic zone, but China claims almost the entire sea as its own. The Philippines keeps a small marine garrison on a deliberately grounded, rusting warship there to assert its claim; China's coast guard regularly harasses supply missions to it with water cannons and blocking maneuvers. In 2016, an international tribunal ruled decisively that China's sweeping claim has no legal basis — a ruling Beijing has ignored ever since.

stories.title: Trump unveils a phased tariff plan on generic drugs — up to 200% within three years
stories.what_happened: President Trump announced that imported generic drugs will face 0% tariffs for the next two years (effective August 1, 2026), rising to 100% for a third year, and 200% after that — explicitly designed to give foreign manufacturers a window to build US plants or face escalating penalties. This is separate from tariffs on large branded pharmaceutical companies' imports, which take effect July 31 for a list of 17 major drugmakers. Trump's statement did not name specific countries, companies, or how exemptions (for those who do start building US plants) would be verified.
key_points: Generic drug imports face 0% tariffs for 2 years, then 100%, then 200% after that
Aim: force overseas generic drugmakers to build US factories or pay steep penalties
Separately, tariffs on big branded/patented drugmakers' imports already start July 31
No countries or companies named yet, and no exemption details given
India, the world's largest supplier of generic medicines, has the most at stake

depth.background: A 'generic' drug is a cheaper copy of a brand-name medicine, sold once the original's patent expires — most pills Americans take (and most global medicine supply) are generics, and a huge share are made in India and, to a lesser extent, China. The Trump administration has spent 2026 rolling out tariffs (an extra tax on imported goods, paid by the importer and usually passed on in prices) on pharmaceuticals in stages, first targeting big branded-drug makers, and has repeatedly threatened action on generics to bring manufacturing back to the US ('reshoring').

stories.title: Yemen's Houthis open a second shipping front, blockading the Red Sea's Bab al-Mandeb Strait
stories.what_happened: This week the Houthis announced a full naval blockade of Saudi Arabia, using the threat of missile and drone strikes near Bab al-Mandeb to force ships away. Within days, at least seven tankers bound for Saudi ports reversed course rather than risk it, and a Cosco-operated Chinese vehicle carrier turned back after receiving a direct warning from Houthi forces. Some vessels are now taking the much longer route around via the Suez Canal instead. The Joint Maritime Information Center — the body that warns commercial sailors of threats — told mariners the Houthis have finished positioning weapons near the strait, though no ship has actually been struck yet.
key_points: Houthis declare a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia via the Bab al-Mandeb Strait
At least 7 oil tankers have already turned around rather than risk it
A Chinese vehicle carrier reversed course after a Houthi warning email
Missiles and drones are reportedly positioned near the strait, but no ship has been hit yet
This opens a SECOND global shipping chokepoint crisis on top of the Strait of Hormuz

depth.background: Bab al-Mandeb ('Gate of Tears') is the narrow strait between Yemen and the Horn of Africa that roughly 10% of global seaborne trade passes through on its way to and from the Suez Canal. Yemen's Houthi rebels, an armed group backed by Iran, have attacked Red Sea shipping before (2023-2025) in what they called solidarity with Gaza. That campaign quieted down earlier this year. But the US and Iran have been at war for weeks over the OTHER key chokepoint, the Strait of Hormuz (where a fifth of the world's oil passes) — and the Houthis are Iran's ally.

stories.title: India and the US race to close a trade deal before Thursday's tariff deadline — India still holding out
stories.what_happened: Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal completed a two-day round of talks with US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, with both sides calling the progress 'substantial.' Washington has already cut its reciprocal tariff on Indian goods from 25% to 18% as talks progressed. But no deal has been signed, and reports describe the legal text as sitting at the 'last 1 per cent.' India is deliberately not rushing to meet the July 24 deadline, instead pushing for tariff terms more competitive than those given to Vietnam, Indonesia and other Asian exporters it competes with.
key_points: Interim US tariff arrangement (including an extra 10% levy) expires July 24
Deal described as being at the 'last 1%' of legal text, but still unsigned
India wants better tariff terms than Asian rivals get, not just any deal by the deadline
Washington already cut its reciprocal tariff on Indian goods from 25% to 18%
Goal on both sides: $500 billion in two-way trade by 2030 ('Mission 500')

depth.background: Since April 2026, the US has run a 'reciprocal tariff' regime — extra import taxes matched roughly to what other countries charge US goods — with a temporary lower rate for countries actively negotiating trade deals. India has been negotiating a first-phase Bilateral Trade Agreement with the US covering market access, digital trade rules, and non-tariff barriers (rules and standards, rather than tariffs, that make imports harder), aiming to eventually double trade to $500 billion by 2030.

stories.title: Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi and Akhilesh Yadav detained, then freed, after a sit-in outside PM Modi's residence
stories.what_happened: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, his sister Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, and Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav led a sit-in protest march from Rajaji Marg to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's residence at 7 Lok Kalyan Marg, demanding accountability for police action against students and the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Delhi Police forcibly removed the protesters: Rahul Gandhi sat on the road and was carried by several officers into a police bus, while Priyanka Gandhi Vadra was pushed into a bus as well. Senior Congress figures including Mallikarjun Kharge also joined. All those detained were released later that evening; former Congress president Sonia Gandhi visited Priyanka before her release.
key_points: Top opposition leaders sat down on the road outside Modi's official residence, refusing to move
Delhi Police physically carried Rahul Gandhi and pushed Priyanka Gandhi into a police bus
Akhilesh Yadav (Samajwadi Party chief) was also forcibly removed
Demand: resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the NEET-UG paper leak
All were released hours later; Sonia Gandhi visited Priyanka before her release

depth.background: This escalation sits inside a much bigger story we've been tracking: the 'Cockroach' movement — a student-led protest movement that grew out of anger over India's NEET-UG medical entrance exam, after its 2026 paper was leaked and about 2.2 million students had to retake it under heavy security. A youth march ('Chalo Sansad') toward Parliament days earlier was met with tear gas and baton charges, injuring students, which is what pulled the opposition's top leadership into the streets themselves.

thread.previously: We explained how a joke about students calling themselves 'cockroaches' (able to survive anything) grew into the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party movement demanding accountability over the NEET paper leak.
thread.changed: The movement's demands have now pulled in the national opposition leadership directly — Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi and Akhilesh Yadav were themselves detained by police outside the PM's residence, escalating this from a youth protest into a full opposition-versus-government confrontation.

prev_ref.title: India's 'Cockroach' movement, explained: how a joke about students became a nationwide challenge to Modi

stories.title: Aston Martin's biggest upgrade of the season lands in Hungary — new chassis, new nose, reworked aero
stories.what_happened: Aston Martin has confirmed its single biggest upgrade package of the season will run for the first time at this weekend's Hungarian Grand Prix: a re-homologated (formally re-certified with the FIA) lighter chassis, a new nose, and reworked aerodynamics, all designed under Newey. The upgrade lands on a Hungaroring circuit that has also had sections resurfaced at Turns 1 and 12, adding another variable for every team to adapt to.
key_points: Package includes a re-homologated (re-certified) lighter chassis, new nose and reworked aerodynamics
Designed by Adrian Newey, F1's most decorated car designer, in his first full season at Aston Martin
Arrives after a difficult season for the team and Newey's own recent health scare
Comes on newly resurfaced sections of the Hungaroring (Turns 1 and 12)

depth.background: We've been following Aston Martin's rocky 2026 season and the pressure on Adrian Newey, the legendary designer behind championship-winning cars at Williams, McLaren and Red Bull, who joined Aston Martin to help engineer a turnaround. His future — and that of driver Fernando Alonso, a two-time champion weighing whether to keep racing — has been tied to whether this promised 'big upgrade' actually delivers on track.

thread.previously: Newey had said his major upgrade for Aston Martin would arrive at the Hungarian Grand Prix, after a difficult season and his own health scare.
thread.changed: The upgrade's specifics are now confirmed: a re-homologated lighter chassis, new nose and reworked aero — the team's biggest single package of 2026, arriving on a freshly resurfaced Hungaroring.

prev_ref.title: Adrian Newey says his big Aston Martin upgrade lands in Hungary — after a torrid season and his own health scare

stories.title: Antonelli's championship lead grows to 45 points as Russell slips to third after a scoreless Spa
stories.what_happened: After Antonelli's win at Spa-Francorchamps (his sixth of the season), the standings now read: Antonelli 204 points, Hamilton 159, and Russell a further 50 points back in third after retiring from Spa with zero points, following a collision with Hamilton on the opening lap. Heading into the Hungarian Grand Prix — round 11 of 2026, and the final race before F1's four-week summer shutdown — Antonelli holds a commanding 45-point cushion.
key_points: Antonelli: 204 points, Hamilton: 159, Russell now a further 50 points back
Russell failed to score at Spa after a first-lap collision with former teammate Hamilton
This flips the story we told earlier this week — Hamilton, not Russell, now clearly F1's #2
Hungary is the last race before F1's 4-week summer break — a title cushion matters more now

depth.background: We've been tracking the emerging title fight between Mercedes rookie sensation Kimi Antonelli and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, whose 2026 form has surged after a rocky start following his Ferrari move. George Russell, Antonelli's Mercedes teammate, had also been in that mix — but a first-lap incident at the Belgian Grand Prix (Spa) involving Hamilton has now dropped him well behind both.

thread.previously: We reported Hamilton's Ferrari turnaround had lifted him to third in the drivers' standings, chasing an eighth title.
thread.changed: The picture has since clarified: Hamilton is actually second, not third — it's Russell who has dropped to third after scoring zero points at Spa, and Antonelli's lead has grown to a commanding 45 points.
